strengths: The paper identifies and systematically demonstrates a previously unexplored attack surface: pruning as an activation mechanism for malicious behavior in LLMs. The core insight—that pruning scores correlate across algorithms and can be estimated by an adversary—is sound and enables a robust attack that triggers under all three vLLM pruning algorithms without knowing the user's configuration.

The evaluation is extensive and convincing: 5 instruction-tuned models, 3 attack scenarios (jailbreak, over-refusal, content injection), 7 pruning configurations, utility preservation checks (5 benchmarks), benign refusal rate checks, and ablations on the repair ratio (α_rep). Attack success rates exceeding 90% in many settings with low pre-pruning ASR strongly support the central claims.

The analysis goes beyond demonstrating the attack: §6.2 empirically validates the key assumption (>99% of repaired parameters are actually pruned, with per-setting results in Table 9), and §6.3 provides a thoughtful examination of defenses (security-aware calibration, patching), including honest negative results (practical patching is largely ineffective, security-aware calibration has utility costs and is insufficient).

The threat model is realistic and well-motivated, grounded in actual vLLM functionality (users pruning downloaded models), and the paper is clearly positioned relative to quantization-activated and fine-tuning-activated attacks, showing what is genuinely new.
Reproducibility support is good: full hyperparameters, dataset construction details, judge prompts, and a statement that code and configuration files will be released.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental. The work directly imports the 'post-training transformation-activated backdoor' paradigm from Egashira et al. (2024, 2025) and Gloaguen et al. (2025) to pruning, and the attack mechanics (inject in frozen-protected parameters, repair in to-be-pruned parameters) are a fairly straightforward adaptation. The main technical novelty is the Wanda-score-based parameter selection, which is a simple heuristic.

The threat model assumes the adversary has full white-box access, can fine-tune the checkpoint before release, and that users will download a fine-tuned third-party model and then prune it in vLLM. The practical prevalence of this exact pipeline is asserted rather than evidenced, and the adversary must also successfully publish such a model on a hub—raising questions about real-world exploitability compared to data-poisoning alternatives.

Results are uneven in places: SparseGPT 20% ASR is low for some models (e.g., 22.0% for Llama, 9.1–24.9% for content injection), and the 2:4 configurations show high variance. The paper acknowledges this only briefly; a deeper explanation of failure modes (beyond the iterative compensation hypothesis) would strengthen the analysis.

The evaluation relies on GPT-4.1-mini as an LLM judge for jailbreak and over-refusal ASR without human validation of judge agreement; refusal/harmfulness scoring via LLM judges can be noisy, and no inter-rater statistics are reported.

Defense analysis is largely discussion-level: no proposed mitigation is evaluated against an adaptive attacker, so the claimed severity of the 'deployment-time security gap' is not fully stress-tested against the most obvious countermeasures (e.g., pruning with attacker-unpredictable calibration data distributions at scale, or post-pruning safety audits).

strengths: Well-motivated and realistic threat model grounded in an actual deployment pipeline (vLLM's integrated pruning algorithms), making the security question practically relevant rather than purely hypothetical.

The core mechanism is sensible and clearly articulated: pre-estimating pruning scores with Wanda as a proxy, injecting malicious behavior into parameters unlikely to be pruned, and 'repairing' the model via parameters likely to be pruned so the attack stays dormant until pruning.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 5 models, 3 attack scenarios, 3 pruning algorithms, 7 pruning configurations (including 2:4 semi-structured), with utility preservation verified on 5 standard benchmarks and benign refusal rates reported.

Useful analysis beyond the main result: ablation of the repair-set size (αrep), quantitative analysis of the adversary's pruning-score estimation accuracy (>99% of repaired parameters pruned in most cases, Table 9), and initial defense exploration (security-aware calibration, patching experiments).
Clear writing, good use of figures/tables, reproducibility statement with promised code release, and an ethics statement addressing dual-use concerns.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the attack is a direct adaptation of existing post-training transformation attacks (Egashira et al. 2024/2025 on quantization; Gloaguen et al. 2025 on fine-tuning) to pruning. The inject-then-repair recipe and threat model are essentially inherited; the only genuinely new ingredient is pre-estimating pruning scores, which is a fairly natural observation given the known correlation between pruning metrics.

The key enabling insight largely reconfirms prior findings rather than establishing new ones: Wei et al. (2024) already showed safety alignment is brittle under pruning, so the fact that pruning removes a lightly-trained 'repair' is a somewhat expected consequence, weakening the significance of the technical contribution.

Attack robustness is overstated relative to the evidence. Success rates vary widely across configurations: e.g., jailbreak ASR for Llama3.1-8B under SparseGPT 20% is only 22% (vs. 6% base), and content injection ASR under SparseGPT 20% drops to 9-25% for several models. Several cells in Table 2 are close to or barely above base ASR, which contradicts the framing of the attack as 'consistent' and 'robust to configuration choices'.

Defense analysis is thin and somewhat optimistic-critical imbalance: security-aware calibration essentially eliminates SparseGPT-based attacks (ASR ~0.1-3.7%), yet the paper concludes defenses are 'insufficient' based mainly on Wanda's resistance. No exploration of other natural defenses (e.g., post-pruning fine-tuning, output screening, pruning with diverse calibration data) that users could actually apply.

Evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini) for both jailbreak harmfulness and refusal classification, with no human validation or inter-annotator agreement reported; the over-refusal scenario in particular is susceptible to judge miscalibration given the broad 'refusal with reasons' criterion.

Attack scenarios have limited real-world severity: content injection via 'McDonald's' keyword spam and generic over-refusal are more proof-of-concept than compelling threat demonstrations, and the adversarially rewritten AutoPoison datasets (tuned specifically to maximize ASR) make the reported ASR upper bounds somewhat circular.

The adversary knows/uses vLLM defaults and evaluates only 50% and 20% sparsity with default calibration; sensitivity to other sparsity levels, calibration dataset sizes, or pruning implementations outside vLLM is not examined, so generality claims remain narrow.

Some methodological choices are under-justified: why Wanda scores alone suffice as a proxy for all three methods is asserted and empirically checked but never analyzed theoretically; the asymmetry between brittle repair (1% parameters) and robust injection (50%) is empirical rather than explained in a principled way.

strengths: Novel and timely security question: the paper is the first to systematically demonstrate that LLM pruning can act as an activation trigger for malicious behavior, extending a line of work on quantization- and fine-tuning-activated attacks (Egashira et al.; Gloaguen et al.) to a widely used deployment-time transformation with a realistic threat model grounded in vLLM's integrated pruning algorithms.

The core attack idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: pre-estimate pruning scores (Wanda scores) to identify parameters unlikely to be pruned for injection and parameters likely to be pruned for repair, exploiting the empirical correlation of pruning scores across methods. This is a clean, generalizable mechanism.

Comprehensive evaluation: 5 instruction-tuned models, 3 attack scenarios (jailbreak, over-refusal, content injection), 7 pruning configurations per scenario, and utility preservation verified on 5 standard benchmarks. The extensive appendix tables (Tables 5-9) provide transparency.

Useful analysis beyond the main results: ablation on the repair set size (Section 6.1) with per-scenario interpretation, empirical validation that >99% of repair parameters are actually pruned (Section 6.2, Table 9), and a defense discussion (Section 6.3) including a security-aware calibration experiment and a patching analysis that honestly reports the limits of practical defenses.

Stealthiness is properly assessed: unpruned attacked models match base models on benchmarks and benign refusal rates, and the paper acknowledges that pruning itself can modestly raise ASR on base models, correctly separating this from the attack effect.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction (including prompts), evaluation protocols, judge prompts, and a code release commitment.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to prior post-training transformation attacks: the threat model, attack scenarios, and evaluation methodology closely mirror Egashira et al. (2024, 2025) and Gloaguen et al. (2025); the main new element is the pruning-score estimation plus inject/repair split, which is a fairly natural adaptation of known ideas to pruning. The paper is an expected extension of an established research program rather than a conceptual leap.

Attack robustness is weaker than the framing suggests. The abstract and introduction claim the model becomes malicious 'once pruned' with any of the three vLLM algorithms, but Table 2 shows substantial failures in some configurations: e.g., SparseGPT 20% yields only 22.0% jailbreak ASR on Llama and 9.1% content injection ASR on Llama, and several other SparseGPT 20% results are low. The claim of 'success rates exceeding 90% across all three pruning algorithms' does not hold uniformly.

The Magnitude results are unsurprising: since the pruning criterion is simply |W|, an adversary can trivially guarantee injection into unpruned parameters; including it as evidence of generality inflates the perceived difficulty of the attack.

No strong baselines or comparisons: there is no comparison against simpler alternatives (e.g., random-parameter selection for injection/repair, or attacks targeting a single pruning method), which would quantify how much the score-estimation component actually contributes. The ablation studies (alpha_rep, score accuracy) do not substitute for this.

Threat model limitations: the adversary requires white-box access, the ability to fine-tune and release a checkpoint, and knowledge of the exact pruning algorithms integrated in the target engine. The paper does not discuss how the attack degrades if users apply other pruning tools or different implementations/calibration defaults.

Defense analysis is thin and mostly negative (security-aware calibration insufficient; practical patching ineffective). No detection mechanism is proposed or evaluated, so the practical mitigation story is left largely open.

Attack success is partly confounded by pruning-induced degradation: at 50% sparsity and 2:4 settings, pruned models (even base ones) suffer large utility drops (Table 5), and the attacked pruned models also show noticeable benchmark degradation; the practical relevance of attacking heavily degraded configurations is questionable.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated threat: the first demonstration of pruning-activated attacks in LLMs, filling a genuine gap left by prior work on quantization- and fine-tuning-activated backdoors (Egashira et al.; Gloaguen et al.). The threat model is realistic and well-motivated by actual vLLM deployment practices.

Core technical idea (inject malicious behavior into low-pruning-score parameters, then repair via parameters with high pruning probability) is simple, well-reasoned, and effective across all three vLLM pruning algorithms, which requires handling algorithm-heterogeneity (Magnitude/Wanda/SparseGPT) without knowing user configuration.

Extensive and convincing evaluation: 5 models (plus larger 14B/32B models in the appendix), 3 attack scenarios, 7 pruning configurations, utility preservation checks, ablations on αinj/αrep, calibration-dataset robustness, and empirical validation that >99% of repair parameters are actually pruned.

Careful analysis beyond the attack itself: security-aware calibration, parameter patching, sparse fine-tuning, and quantization-after-pruning experiments give a nuanced picture of the defense landscape, with honest reporting that current mitigations are insufficient.
Clear writing, good positioning against related work, explicit ethics and reproducibility statements, and promised code release.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to prior post-training transformation attacks: the paper largely adapts an established recipe (predict which parameters survive a transformation, hide a trigger in them, compensate elsewhere) from quantization/fine-tuning backdoor work to pruning; the conceptual contribution is an application rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The attack relies on a strong white-box threat model (adversary controls the checkpoint and can fine-tune before release); the paper could better discuss how restrictive this is relative to realistic hub-level adversaries and verification pipelines.

Results are somewhat inconsistent in places (e.g., SparseGPT 20%/2:4 ASR varies widely across models, OLMo content injection at Wanda 20% is only 27.3%), and the paper's headline claims of >90% success rates overstate the uniformity across configurations.

Defense analysis is largely empirical and limited; no detection-oriented evaluation (e.g., weight-distribution anomaly tests, pruning-then-check pipelines) beyond re-patching experiments, so the practical risk assessment is only partially quantified.
Evaluation relies on an LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini) without human validation of ASR measurements; also, only unstructured/2:4 sparsity is studied, excluding structured pruning used in some deployments.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely new attack surface: the paper is the first to demonstrate pruning as an activation trigger for dormant malicious behavior in LLMs, complementing prior work on quantization- and fine-tuning-activated attacks and covering an increasingly common deployment step (pruning via vLLM).

The core mechanism is well-motivated and clearly articulated: pre-estimating pruning scores (Wanda proxy) to separate 'injection' parameters (likely retained) from 'repair' parameters (likely pruned) is an elegant way to hide a trigger, and the brittleness asymmetry (tiny repair set) is a clever design choice.

Empirically thorough evaluation: 5 models (plus 14B/32B in appendix), 3 attack scenarios, 3 pruning algorithms, 7 pruning configurations, utility preservation on 5 benchmarks, ablations over alpha_rep and alpha_inj, calibration-dataset mismatch analysis, post-pruning fine-tuning and quantization, and a pruning-score accuracy analysis (Table 12).

Defense discussion is honest rather than hand-wavy: security-aware calibration and parameter patching are tested empirically, with clear statements of their limitations (e.g., optimal patching requires oracle access to pre-attack scores).

Stealthiness is properly verified: the unpruned attacked model shows low ASR and benign refusal rates comparable to the base model, and utility degradation is small, supporting the 'seemingly benign' claim.
Clear threat model that mirrors realistic practice (off-the-shelf pruning in vLLM, adversary has no post-release control), and code is promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty beyond the trigger choice: the recipe (parameter-subset fine-tuning with KL regularization plus a proxy importance score) is a fairly direct adaptation of existing transformation-activated attacks (Egashira et al. 2024/2025 for quantization, Gloaguen et al. 2025 for fine-tuning). The main novelty is the observation that Wanda scores correlate across pruning methods, which is intuitive and empirically confirmed but not a deep technical contribution.

Attack reliability is overstated. The abstract claims consistency across algorithms, but Table 2 shows substantial variance: e.g., jailbreak ASR of only 22.0% (SparseGPT 20%, Llama3.1-8B) and 19.3% (2:4), content injection as low as 4.7-11.0% for Llama under SparseGPT 20%/2:4, and notable drops under calibration mismatch (Table 7: 11.9-28.3% with Open Platypus). The 'robust across any configuration' framing is stronger than the evidence.

A confound is not fully resolved: pruning alone degrades safety for base models (e.g., Mistral base jailbreak ASR rises from 43.7% unpruned to 70.0% under Wanda 2:4; Qwen rises to 25-29%). This makes some 'attack vs. base' deltas harder to attribute cleanly to the injected mechanism, and for already-unsafe models (Mistral) the practical gain from the attack is less clear.

Evaluation relies solely on GPT-4.1-mini as an LLM judge with thresholded 5-point scores and no human validation or judge-agreement analysis, which weakens the ASR measurements, especially for jailbreak and over-refusal judgments.

The content-injection scenario is a weak threat: injecting 'McDonald's' into answers is more of a nuisance/demonstration than a realistic harm, limiting the significance of that portion of the results.

Defenses remain largely open. Security-aware calibration works only partially (it fails for Wanda), and the practical patching variant is ineffective; the paper concedes no reliable mitigation exists, so the constructive contribution beyond demonstrating the threat is limited.
Scope is restricted to unstructured/2:4 pruning in vLLM; other widely used pruning tools and structured pruning methods are untested, so generality of the threat is uncertain.

Dual-use risk: full attack code and constructed poisoning datasets are released with a fairly brief ethics statement; a stronger harm-mitigation justification and responsible-disclosure discussion (e.g., notifying vLLM) would be appropriate.

strengths: First systematic demonstration that LLM pruning can serve as a deployment-time trigger for malicious behavior, extending the post-training transformation attack family (quantization, fine-tuning) to pruning, which is a natural but previously unexplored gap

Realistic and well-motivated threat model grounded in an actual widely-used system (vLLM's default pruning algorithms), including the practical constraint that the adversary does not know which pruning algorithm, sparsity level, or calibration dataset the user will choose

Extensive empirical evaluation: 5 base models (plus larger Qwen2.5-14B/32B), 3 attack scenarios (jailbreak, over-refusal, content injection), 7 pruning configurations, with utility preservation checks (5 benchmarks), benign refusal rates, and a base-model control throughout

Good analysis beyond the headline result: ablations on repair ratio (αrep) and injection ratio (αinj), empirical validation that pruning-score estimation is accurate (>99% of repaired parameters pruned in most cases) and robust to calibration-dataset mismatch, attack persistence under subsequent fine-tuning and quantization

Honest treatment of defenses: security-aware calibration and parameter patching are evaluated and shown to be only partially effective, with clear articulation of the utility-security trade-offs; code release promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the inject-then-repair template is directly adapted from quantization-activated attacks (Egashira et al., 2024; 2025) and fine-tuning-activated backdoors (Gloaguen et al., 2025); the main technical novelty is using Wanda scores as a proxy for prune-likelihood, which is a fairly intuitive adaptation given Wanda's known correlation with other pruning metrics

Attack strength varies considerably across configurations: for several model/algorithm combinations (e.g., SparseGPT 20% for content injection and jailbreak with Llama), ASR drops to 5-25%, so the 'works after any pruning method' claim is only partially supported and the pattern of failures is not deeply analyzed

Part of the post-pruning ASR increase appears attributable to pruning itself degrading base-model safety (base jailbreak ASR rises to ~25-29% under 2:4 pruning), which somewhat inflates the apparent attack effect; the attack's marginal contribution over generic pruning-induced safety degradation deserves sharper quantification

Threat model assumes a knowledgeable adversary (white-box access, ability to simulate pruning locally) but a credulous victim (users prune models from unknown publishers with no verification); practical adoption likelihood and mitigations at the hub level (e.g., model signing, publishing both pruned/unpruned variants) are not discussed

Defense analysis is limited to two heuristic mitigations on one scenario; no detection method (e.g., pruning-and-checking as in fine-pruning-style defenses, or weight-difference analysis) is evaluated, which would strengthen the security contribution

Some utility degradation is non-trivial in places (e.g., -2.9 ± 5.2 average benchmark change for the Qwen jailbreak attack), which weakens the 'seemingly benign' claim in the worst cases; statistical significance of benchmark changes is not assessed
Only single-seed results appear to be reported; ASR variance and LLM-judge reliability are not quantified
